title: Naked cake and semi-naked cake
subtitle: Applying a deliberately thin frosting to show the sponge layers through the sides
excerpt: A naked cake has no side frosting; a semi-naked cake has a thin, scraped-back coat that lets the sponge show through. Both rely on level layers and a firm, structured filling. The result reads as relaxed but the preparation is not.
sourceNotes: The naked cake style became widely practised in the UK and US from around 2013 and has been covered extensively in food publications. The structural principles (level sponge, firm filling, stable buttercream temperature) are the same as for fully frosted cakes; only the exterior is intentionally exposed.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble and chill the cake the day before, covered loosely. Add flowers, fruit, or garnishes on the day.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cake style where buttercream or cream cheese frosting is applied to the side in a thin coat and then scraped back so the sponge layers are partially visible through the frosting.

content.text: look requires level layers and a filling that does not squeeze out under the weight of the stack. The style looks unstructured but depends on the same discipline as a fully frosted cake: cold sponge, firm filling, and scraping at the right temperature.

A naked cake cannot hide an uneven layer beneath frosting, so levelling matters more than for a fully covered cake. Use a long serrated knife or a cake leveller. Lay a ruler against the side of the cake and trim any dome from the top of each layer. Work cold: a sponge from the fridge cuts more cleanly than a room-temperature one.

Spread buttercream or whipped cream to a consistent thickness on each layer, right to the edge but no further. Place the next layer and press lightly. If the filling is soft (jam, cream, lemon curd), pipe a buttercream dam around the edge of each layer before filling; this stops the soft filling pushing out when the layers are stacked.
Chill the stacked cake for 20 minutes. Apply a coat of buttercream to the sides with a palette knife, covering the whole surface.

Hold an icing smoother upright against the side of the cake. Rotate the turntable in one slow, steady movement, pressing gently. The smoother removes most of the buttercream and leaves a thin, translucent layer showing the sponge beneath.
Clean the smoother between each pass. Two or three passes bring the coat to an even thinness where the sponge shows through but the surface is smooth.

Spread a thin layer of buttercream on the top and smooth with the palette knife. For a fully naked cake, skip the sides entirely and use only a thin scrape on the top edge to stop crumbs falling. Chill the finished cake for 30 minutes before adding fresh flowers, berries, or other garnishes.
